opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think the honest answer is that it's still quite crude right now, but it's getting better.

At a high level, what you'd ideally want is for the model to allocate compute roughly in proportion to the marginal value of thinking more. For an easy question, like "what's the capital of France?", there's basically no return to reasoning for thousands of tokens. You know the answer, you should just say it. For a hard math problem or a tricky coding task, the returns to extra reasoning can be very large: you can try different approaches, check your work, backtrack when something doesn't pan out.

In practice, a lot of this comes out of training. When you do reinforcement learning on reasoning tasks, the model gets rewarded for getting the right answer, and often there's some implicit or explicit pressure on length or cost. So the model learns heuristics: this looks like the kind of problem where I tend to make mistakes, so I should slow down, verify, consider alternatives. It's somewhat analogous to how a person develops a sense of when a problem is "hard" and deserves careful thought versus when they can just answer from intuition.

There are also more explicit mechanisms. Developers expose settings like "reasoning effort" or thinking budgets, so the user or the application decides how much compute to throw at something. And you can imagine routing systems, where a cheaper model or a classifier first estimates difficulty and then decides whether to escalate to a more expensive reasoning mode.

My sense is that the models are still fairly miscalibrated here. They sometimes overthink trivial things and underthink things that are actually subtle, partly because judging difficulty in advance is itself a hard problem. You often don't know a problem is hard until you've started working on it. So I'd expect a lot of progress to come from models that monitor their own progress: noticing they're stuck, or noticing they've converged, and adjusting dynamically rather than committing to a budget up front.

And economically this matters a lot. If inference compute becomes a large share of total AI compute, which I think is plausible, then how efficiently models allocate that thinking time translates pretty directly into how much useful work you get per dollar. So getting this right is not just a nice-to-have, it's a big lever on the overall productivity of these systems.

r001.rationale: The response discusses allocating inference compute by difficulty and dynamically adjusting effort, but it does not mention or describe speculative decoding or allocating more large-model computation through it.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think it's worth separating two things here. There's the question of how it currently works in practice, and then there's the question of how a well-designed system should work, and those are pretty different.

Right now, the honest answer is that it's mostly not the model deciding. It's the developer. When you look at how the labs deploy these reasoning models, there's typically some setting, a "reasoning effort" parameter or a token budget, that gets chosen either by the lab or exposed to the user as a knob. And then the model has been trained with reinforcement learning to produce chains of thought that roughly fit within those budgets. So the model does have some learned sense of when to stop thinking, but it's a fairly coarse sense, and it's heavily shaped by the training distribution rather than by a careful assessment of the marginal value of another thousand tokens on this particular question.

And you can see this in the failure modes. Models will sometimes spend an enormous amount of compute on a trivial arithmetic question, or they'll stop early on something genuinely hard. The allocation isn't that well calibrated to difficulty, and it's certainly not calibrated to how much the answer actually matters to the user.

Now, what should happen in principle is kind of an economics problem. You have some value of getting the answer right, you have some cost per unit of compute, and the right amount of inference is where the marginal improvement in expected answer quality equals the marginal cost. That's just a standard optimization. The hard part is that the model would need to estimate, before it's done the work, how much extra thinking is likely to improve the answer. That's a form of metacognition that I don't think current systems do very well.

What's interesting to me is that this is going to become much more important as inference compute becomes a larger share of total AI spending. We've done some work at Epoch looking at the scaling of inference compute, and you can get quite large capability gains from spending more at inference time, but the returns do diminish, and it's often log-linear or worse. So if you're spending ten or a hundred times more compute on a question, you want to be quite confident it's worth it. And I'd expect that over the next few years you see much more sophisticated approaches, where models are explicitly trained to make this allocation decision, maybe with some notion of the value of the task baked in. But today, it's much more of a blunt instrument than people might assume.

r001.rationale: The response discusses inference-compute budgets and possible future allocation based on task value, but does not mention speculative decoding or say it dynamically gives harder problems more large-model computation.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two slightly different questions here. One is how much compute we, as the people deploying the model, allow it to use. The other is how the model decides to use that budget. You might give it a limit on how many tokens it can generate, but within that limit it can spend more or less time working through a problem before producing an answer.

One way to learn that behavior is through reinforcement learning. If spending longer on a difficult problem leads to a correct answer, that behavior can be rewarded. If you also put a cost on computation, then you create an incentive to answer easy questions quickly and spend more effort on questions where additional reasoning actually helps.

The tricky part is that the model has to judge whether more thinking is likely to be useful. Being uncertain doesn't necessarily mean that more computation will resolve the uncertainty—you might just be missing some information. So ideally, what it learns is something like: what's the expected benefit of doing another step of reasoning, relative to the cost? I wouldn't assume that models make that calculation explicitly, but training can push their behavior in that direction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses spending more reasoning effort on difficult problems, but attributes this to learned behavior and reinforcement learning. It does not mention speculative decoding or suggest that it dynamically allocates large-model computation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a couple of different mechanisms. One is that the amount of compute is determined by the system around the model. You might have a fixed budget for how many tokens it can generate, or you might sample several answers and use another model to select among them. In those cases, the model itself isn’t necessarily deciding how much effort to spend.

But with reasoning models, there is also a learned decision about how long to keep working before producing an answer. During training, the model can be rewarded for getting the answer right, and potentially penalized for taking too long. That creates an incentive to spend more compute when additional reasoning is likely to help, and to stop when it isn’t.

The difficult part is knowing when that extra reasoning will actually be useful. A model can spend a lot of tokens going around in circles. So generating a longer chain of reasoning isn’t, by itself, evidence that it’s allocating compute well. Ideally, it would learn to recognize which problems need more work and when it has reached a point where further computation has little value.

r001.rationale: The response discusses fixed token budgets, sampling, and learned stopping decisions, but never mentions speculative decoding or says it dynamically allocates more large-model computation to harder problems.
